about: Building types (roadmap BT1d): estate and garden buildings: gatehouses and lodges, stables and coach houses, glasshouses, garden buildings, mausolea. Same fields as lineage.json.

types.name: Gatehouse

period.text: fortified gateways from the Bronze Age into modern times (no early isles example dated in the sources); the earliest standing in the isles that the sources date is the Balkerne Gate, Colchester, probably 2nd century AD; still built

types.structure: a gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch, flanking towers holding stairs and rooms
types.note: The general type: gatehouses of castles, monasteries, manors and colleges are its variants. FISH files castle, abbey, priory and friary gatehouses under it.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Fortified gates or gateways appear in the Bronze Age and reach into the modern times.

sources.title: Balkerne Gate
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: According to Historic England, the gate probably dates to the 2nd century AD.

sources.title: Balkerne Gate
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is the largest surviving gateway in Roman Britain and was built where the Roman road from Londinium intersected the town wall of Camulodunum.

sources.title: Gatehouse (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70372)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch; the flanking towers housing stairs and additional rooms. Use with wider site type where known.

types.name: Castle gatehouse

period.text: from the Norman conquest: the early Norman gatehouse of Exeter (Rougemont) Castle, begun in or shortly after 1068; at the end of the Middle Ages gatehouses became grand entrances to manor houses (c. 1500 used as the end)

types.structure: the most strongly defended part of the castle: drawbridge, portcullises, machicolations, arrow loops and murder-holes
types.note: FISH has no concept of its own: 'Castle Gatehouse' is a non-preferred term of both GATEHOUSE (70372) and CASTLE (68833).

sources.title: Exeter Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was built into the northern corner of the Roman city walls starting in or shortly after the year 1068, following Exeter's rebellion against William the Conqueror.

sources.title: Exeter Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The castle is named after the red stone found in the hill, and used in the construction of the original buildings, of which the large early Norman gatehouse is the main remaining feature.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: At the end of the Middle Ages, many gatehouses in England and France were converted into beautiful, grand entrance structures to manor houses or estates.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Strongly fortified medieval gatehouses may include a drawbridge, one or more portcullises, machicolations, arrow loops and murder-holes where stones would be dropped on attackers.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Gatehouses are often the most heavily defended section of a fortification, as the gate was the easiest point for an enemy to attack.

types.name: Gatehouse keep

period.text: Tonbridge Castle's twin-towered gatehouse, completed 1260 after 30 years' work; much used in Edward I's Welsh castles, the last Beaumaris, where work stopped in 1330

types.plan: two massive D-shaped towers flanking the entrance passage (the 'Tonbridge style'), with rooms on the floors above
types.note: Whether the upper floors were the constable's lodging (Taylor) or used otherwise (Ashbee) is debated for Harlech.

sources.title: Tonbridge Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Construction of the gatehouse took 30 years, being completed in 1260.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The gatehouse-keep was greatly used in the Welsh castles of Edward I.

sources.title: Beaumaris Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This work finally halted in 1330 with the castle still not built to its intended height; by the end of the project, £15,000 had been spent, a colossal sum for the period.

sources.title: Harlech Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The gatehouse follows the design, sometimes termed the Tonbridge-style, that became popular during the 13th century, with two massive "D-shaped" defensive towers flanking the entrance.

sources.title: Harlech Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The use of these rooms has been the subject of academic debate: historian Arnold Taylor argued that the first floor of the gatehouse was used by the constable as living accommodation, with the second floor used by senior visitors; Jeremy Ashbee has since challenged this interpretation, suggesting the high status accommodation may instead have been in the inner ward, and the gatehouse used for other purposes.

types.name: Monastic gatehouse

period.text: Bury St Edmunds' Norman Gate, 1120-1148, the earliest dated in the sources; its 14th-century Abbey Gate and Thornton Abbey's gatehouse the grandest; ended with the Dissolution, 1539

types.note: FISH files abbey, priory, friary and monastery gatehouses as non-preferred terms of GATEHOUSE (70372).

sources.title: Bury St Edmunds Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Norman Gate dates from 1120 to 1148 and was designed to be the gateway for the Abbey Church and it is still the belfry for the Church of St James, the present cathedral of Bury St Edmunds.

sources.title: Bury St Edmunds Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Abbey Gate is an impressive 14th-century stone gatehouse, designed to be the gateway for the Great Courtyard.

sources.title: Thornton Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Its ruins are a Grade I listed building, including notably England's largest and most impressive surviving monastic gatehouse.

sources.title: Thornton Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The abbey was closed in 1539 by Henry VIII as part of the Dissolution of the Monasteries.

types.name: Tudor and Jacobean gatehouse

period.text: Oxburgh Hall, licence to crenellate 1482, 'the most prominent of the English brick gatehouses of the 15th century'; Layer Marney under Henry VIII; Burton Agnes c. 1610; Stanway's Jacobean gateway of 1630 the latest in the sources

types.structure: a show of castle defences, symbolic rather than real: tall flanking towers, crenellations, often brick
types.note: The same pattern served the colleges: St John's College, Cambridge, Great Gate follows those of Christ's and Queens'.

sources.title: Oxburgh Hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The hall was built for Sir Edmund Bedingfeld who obtained a licence to crenellate in 1482.

sources.title: Oxburgh Hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The entrance, reached by a three-arched bridge on the north side, is through a fortified gatehouse, described by Nikolaus Pevsner as "the most prominent of the English brick gatehouses of the 15th century".

sources.title: Layer Marney Tower
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Constructed in the first half of the reign of Henry VIII, Layer Marney Tower is in many ways the apotheosis of the Tudor gatehouse, and is the tallest example in Britain.

sources.title: Burton Agnes Hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The gatehouse was completed around 1610 and is a grade I listed building.

sources.title: Stanway House
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The triple-gabled Jacobean gateway was created by Paul's son, Sir Richard Tracy, in 1630.

sources.title: Oxburgh Hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The gate was designed to evoke the owner's power and prestige, though as fortification its value is largely symbolic; it is flanked by tall polygonal towers rising in seven tiers, with symmetrical wings extending either side that reveal nothing on the exterior of their differing internal arrangements.

sources.title: St John's College, Cambridge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: St John's Great Gate follows the contemporary pattern employed previously at Christ's College and Queens' College.

period.text: fashionable in the Georgian era with landscape gardens; Worcester Lodge, Badminton, 1748, the earliest built example named (the porter's lodge at Denbigh Castle and New College, Oxford, are cited as antecedents); Eccleston Hill Lodge, 1881, the latest; out of use in the early 20th century (1914 used as the end)

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A notable mid-18th century example is the Worcester Lodge at Badminton House, Gloucestershire, designed in 1748 by William Kent for the Duke of Beaufort.

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: An example of such a Gothic Revival lodge is Eccleston Hill Lodge on the Eaton Hall estate in Cheshire, designed by John Douglas in 1881.

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Originally intended as the office and accommodation for a gatekeeper who was employed by the landowner to control access to the property, they fell out of use in the early 20th century but surviving examples are often preserved and can sometimes be used as domestic housing.

sources.title: Gate Lodge (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 68971)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A dwelling, located at the entrance, or gates, to an estate or park, etc.

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The accommodation inside a lodge was generally rather small, sometimes consisting of only two rooms.

types.name: Stable

period.text: stables are ancient (Pi-Ramesses, 13th century BC); free-standing stables near the house from the 16th century (1500 used); still built

types.structure: in Great Britain traditionally a hayloft on the upper floor with a pitching door at the front
types.plan: divided into stalls, usually with a large stall for a foaling mare or a sick horse

sources.title: Stable
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Free-standing stables began to be built from the 16th century.

sources.title: Stable
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They were well built and placed near the house since these animals were highly valued and carefully maintained.

sources.title: Stable (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70413)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A building in which horses are accommodated.

sources.title: Stable
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Traditionally, stables in Great Britain had a hayloft on the upper floor and a pitching door at the front.

sources.title: Stable
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Their interiors were divided into stalls and usually included a large stall for a foaling mare or sick horse.

types.name: Coach house (carriage house)

period.text: no earlier than the coach, adopted in England by the late 16th century (1580 used; the sources date no early coach house); built with stables and in mews until motor cars replaced horses in the early 20th century (1914 used as the end), then turned into garages

types.note: FISH has CARRIAGE HOUSE (70259) beside COACH HOUSE; the catalogue's 'carriage house' class maps here.

sources.title: Coach House (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70261)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: An outbuilding where a horse-drawn carriage is kept.

sources.title: Carriage House (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70259)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: An outbuilding used for the storage and maintenance of horse-drawn carriages.

sources.title: Coach (carriage)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the late 16th century coaches had spread across the continent and were adopted in England, where they became a standard vehicle for aristocratic travel.

sources.title: Mews
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A mews is a row or courtyard of stables and carriage houses with living quarters above them, built behind large city houses before motor vehicles replaced horses in the early twentieth century.

sources.title: Mews
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: After the Second World War, mews were replaced by alleys and the carriage houses by garages for automobiles.

types.name: Orangeries of Italy and the Continent

period.text: Padua, 1545, the earliest in the sources; spread from the Renaissance gardens of Italy to the Netherlands and France; Versailles, 1684-1686, the largest (the latest the sources date before the type was taken up in England)

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: As early as 1545, an orangery was built in Padua, Italy.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The orangery originated from the Renaissance gardens of Italy, when glass-making technology enabled sufficient expanses of clear glass to be produced.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Known in Italy as limonaia, these early structures employed wood panels or open galleries to protect from the cold.

sources.title: Orangerie of Versailles
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Versailles Orangerie (French: L'orangerie du château de Versailles) was built by Jules Hardouin-Mansart between 1684 and 1686, before work on the Château de Versailles had even begun.

types.name: Orangery

period.text: introduced to English readers by John Parkinson in 1628; Montacute (before c. 1700), Kenwood (c. 1700) and Kensington Palace (1704-1705) the earliest standing; Margam 1787-1793 the longest; still built (Mapperton, 1970)

types.structure: south-facing, on brick or stone bases with brick or stone piers and tall windows, the north wall solid; solid roofs until glazed roofs came in the early 19th century

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In England, John Parkinson introduced the orangery to the readers of his Paradisus in Sole (1628), under the heading "Oranges".

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: An orangery dating from about 1700 is at Kenwood House in London, and a slightly earlier one at Montacute.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The orangery built adjacent to Kensington Palace, believed to be designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor, was constructed between 1704 and 1705.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1970, Victor Montagu constructed an orangery in his formal Italianate gardens at Mapperton, Dorset.

sources.title: Orangery (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69026)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Orangeries were generally built facing south to take advantage of the maximum possible light, and were constructed using brick or stone bases, brick or stone pillars, and a corbel gutter.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The glazed roof, which afforded sunlight to plants that were not dormant, was a development of the early 19th century.

types.name: Glasshouse (greenhouse)

period.text: the greenhouse reached England in the 17th century; the first heated ('stove') greenhouse in the UK was finished at the Chelsea Physic Garden by 1681; the largest built in Victorian England; still built

types.structure: a building made chiefly of glass, used to grow plants and fruit

sources.title: Greenhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The concept of greenhouses also appeared in the Netherlands and then England in the 17th century, along with the plants.

sources.title: Greenhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first 'stove' (heated) greenhouse in the UK was completed at Chelsea Physic Garden by 1681.

sources.title: Greenhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The largest glasshouses yet conceived were constructed in England during the Victorian era.

sources.title: Glasshouse (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70918)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A building made chiefly of glass, used to grow plants and fruit in. Use more specific type where possible.

types.name: Conservatory

period.text: sloped glass in the 18th century (1700 used); the golden age in the 19th century, mainly in England; halted by the Second World War; Victorian-style domestic conservatories again from the 1970s

types.structure: glazed walls and roof (in UK law at least half the side walls and three-quarters of the roof), attached to a house or freestanding; the great public ones of iron and glass

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the 18th century, sloped glass began to be used in conservatory design to allow more light into the structure, enhancing conditions for plant growth.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The 19th century was the golden age of conservatory building, primarily in England.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The widespread construction of UK conservatories came to a halt with the onset of World War II.

sources.title: Conservatory (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69012)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A glasshouse used to grow and display tender decorative plants. May be either an extension to a house or freestanding.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the UK, the legal definition of a conservatory is a building that has at least 50% of its side wall area glazed and at least 75% of its roof glazed with translucent materials, either polycarbonate sheeting or glass.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many of the magnificent public conservatories, built of iron and glass, are the result of this era.

types.name: Palm house

period.text: Belfast Botanic Gardens, finished 1840, one of the earliest; Kew, 1844-1848, the first on its scale; built as status symbols in Victorian Britain (the end of the reign, 1901, used as the end)

types.structure: ornate glass and iron; Kew's the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron

sources.title: Palm House, Kew Gardens
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: One of the earliest examples of a palm house is located in the Belfast Botanic Gardens.

sources.title: Palm House, Kew Gardens
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Designed by Charles Lanyon, the building was completed in 1840.

sources.title: Palm House, Kew Gardens
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was built between 1844 and 1848.

sources.title: Palm House, Kew Gardens
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Initially built as status symbols in Victorian Britain, several examples of ornate glass and iron greenhouses, often but not always called "the Palm House", can still be found in botanical gardens and parks such as Liverpool's Sefton Park and Stanley Park, and in other countries.

sources.title: Victorian era
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the history of the United Kingdom and the British Empire, the Victorian era was the reign of Queen Victoria, from 20 June 1837 until her death on 22 January 1901, although slightly different definitions are sometimes used.

sources.title: Palm House, Kew Gardens
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was also the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron.

sources.title: Palm House (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 92849)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A greenhouse used for growing palms and/or tropical plants.

period.text: emerged in England in the early 18th century: William Kent's gardens at Chiswick, laid out from 1724, among the first; Capability Brown; Humphry Repton (died 1818) the last great designer of the eighteenth-century style

sources.title: English landscape garden
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The English landscape garden, also called English landscape park or simply the English garden (French: Jardin à l'anglaise; Italian: Giardino all'inglese; German: Englischer Landschaftsgarten; Portuguese: Jardim inglês; Spanish: Jardín inglés), is a style of "landscape" garden which emerged in England in the early 18th century, and spread across Europe, replacing the more formal, symmetrical French formal garden which had emerged in the 17th century as the principal gardening style of Europe.

sources.title: English landscape garden
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Kent created one of the first true English landscape gardens at Chiswick House for Richard Boyle, 3rd Earl of Burlington.

sources.title: English landscape garden
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Humphry Repton (21 April 1752 – 24 March 1818) was the last great English landscape designer of the eighteenth century, often regarded as the successor to Capability Brown.

sources.title: Landscape Park (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69033)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Grounds, usually associated with a country house, laid out so as to produce the effect of natural scenery.

period.text: decorative accents of great estates from the late 16th century (the Triangular Lodge, Rushton, 1593-1597); flourished in the landscape gardens of the 18th century; famine follies in Ireland 1845-1849; Faringdon, 1935, the latest in the sources

sources.title: Folly
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Follies began as decorative accents on the great estates of the late 16th and early 17th centuries, but they flourished especially in the two centuries that followed.

sources.title: Rushton Triangular Lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Triangular Lodge is a folly, designed by Sir Thomas Tresham and constructed between 1593 and 1597 near Rushton, Northamptonshire, England.

sources.title: Folly
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Follies in 18th-century French and English gardens"
sources.quote: Follies (French: fabriques) were an important feature of the English garden and French landscape garden in the 18th century, such as Stowe and Stourhead in England and Ermenonville and the gardens of Versailles in France.

sources.title: Folly
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Great Famine of Ireland of 1845–1849 led to the building of several follies in order to provide relief to the poor without issuing unconditional handouts.

sources.title: Faringdon
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The folly on Folly Hill was designed by Lord Gerald Wellesley, later 7th Duke of Wellington, for Lord Berners, and built in 1935.

sources.title: Folly (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69013)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A structure, often found in 18th century landscape gardens, that demonstrates eccentricity or excess rather than practical purpose. They can take many forms - ruins, sham castles, towers, hermits' cells or grottoes.

types.name: Ice and snow stores of Italy

period.text: snow stored in straw-covered pits at Rome in the 3rd century AD (200 used); the Italian mountain ice kept in caves that travellers saw is not dated in the sources (1619, the first English ice house, used as the end)

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In Rome, in the 3rd century CE, snow was imported from the mountains, stored in straw-covered pits, and sold from snow shops.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Ice houses were introduced to Britain by travellers who had seen similar arrangements in Italy, where peasants collected ice from the mountains and used it to keep food fresh in caves.

types.name: Ice house

period.text: James I's at Greenwich Park, 1619, the first in Britain; many more on 18th-century estates; commercial ice wells to Carlo Gatti's of 1857 and 1863 in London, the latest built in the sources; made needless by artificial ice from about 1900

types.structure: partly underground: in Britain commonly a brick-lined, domed chamber, conical or rounded at the base, with a drain for the meltwater

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: James I commissioned the first modern ice house in 1619 in Greenwich Park and another in Hampton Court in 1625–6.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: During the 18th century, there was an increase in the construction of ice houses, often at large manor houses and their estates.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They were built in 1857 and 1863 by the Swiss entrepreneur Carlo Gatti.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Ice was often imported into the United Kingdom from Scandinavia until the 1920s, although from around 1900 the import of ice declined sharply owing to the development of factories in the UK that produced artificial ice.

sources.title: Icehouse (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71409)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A structure, partly underground, for the preservation of ice for use during warmer weather.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Various types and designs of ice houses exist, but British ice houses were commonly brick-lined, domed structures, with most of their volume underground.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They usually had a drain to take away the meltwater.

period.text: the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, 353-351 BC, which gave the type its name; Roman private mausolea along the roads, such as the tomb of Caecilia Metella (c. 30-10 BC); Constantina's at Rome, c. 350, the latest in the sources; out of use once Christianity was dominant

sources.title: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus or Tomb of Mausolus was a tomb built between 353 and 351 BC in Halicarnassus (present Bodrum, Turkey) for Mausolus, an Anatolian from Caria and a satrap in the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and his sister-wife Artemisia II.

sources.title: Tomb of Caecilia Metella
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The mausoleum was probably built in 30–10 BC by her son who also had the same name, Marcus Licinius Crassus.

sources.title: Santa Costanza
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The mausoleum was built around 350, as shown by excavations in 1992 which discovered an earlier building beneath which may have been the baptistry built by Constantine (at the same time as the funerary hall), in which Constantina and her paternal aunt were baptised by Pope Silvester I (d. 335), as recorded in Liber Pontificalis.

sources.title: Mausoleum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: When Christianity became dominant, mausolea fell out of use.

types.name: Mausoleum

period.text: Hawksmoor's at Castle Howard, 1729-1742, almost certainly the first free-standing mausoleum in Western Europe since the fall of Rome; popular in the early modern and modern periods (Darnley 1786, Hamilton 1840-1858); still built

types.structure: a free-standing monument enclosing a burial chamber, wholly above ground or over a burial vault

sources.title: Nicholas Hawksmoor
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Mausoleum (1729–40) built on the same scale as his London churches, it is almost certainly the first free-standing mausoleum built in Western Europe since the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

sources.title: The Mausoleum, Castle Howard
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was constructed by William Etty from 1729 to 1742, and bastion walls were added by Daniel Garrett.

sources.title: Mausoleum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Later, mausolea became particularly popular in Europe and its colonies during the early modern and modern periods.

sources.title: Mausoleum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Mausolea were historically, and still may be, large and impressive constructions for a deceased leader or other person of importance.

sources.title: Mausoleum (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70087)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A monumental burial place, usually for a single person or family.

sources.title: Mausoleum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A mausoleum (plural: mausolea) is an external free-standing building or standalone structure constructed as a monument enclosing the burial chamber of a deceased person or people.

sources.title: Mausoleum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A mausoleum encloses a burial chamber either wholly above ground or within a burial vault below the superstructure.

links.claim: The castle gatehouse is the gatehouse made the strongest point of a fortification, the gate being the easiest point to attack.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Gatehouses are often the most heavily defended section of a fortification, as the gate was the easiest point for an enemy to attack.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A gatehouse is a building that contains the entrance to a large structure or complex, such as a walled town, castle, manor, monastery or academic college, enabling the entrance to be controlled or defended by the inhabitants.

links.claim: Monasteries are among the enclosed places whose entrance a gatehouse controlled; FISH files abbey and priory gatehouses under the gatehouse.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A gatehouse is a building that contains the entrance to a large structure or complex, such as a walled town, castle, manor, monastery or academic college, enabling the entrance to be controlled or defended by the inhabitants.

sources.title: Gatehouse (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70372)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch; the flanking towers housing stairs and additional rooms. Use with wider site type where known.

links.claim: In some castles the gatehouse was fortified so strongly that it took on the function of the keep; the twin D-towered 'Tonbridge style' became popular in the 13th century and was much used in Edward I's Welsh castles.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In some castles, the gatehouse was so strongly fortified it took on the function of a keep, sometimes referred to as a "gatehouse keep".

sources.title: Harlech Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The gatehouse follows the design, sometimes termed the Tonbridge-style, that became popular during the 13th century, with two massive "D-shaped" defensive towers flanking the entrance.

links.claim: The great monastic gatehouses of the 14th century carried castle defences: Bury St Edmunds' Abbey Gate keeps its portcullis and Thornton's is approached over a fortified bridge. The sources describe the defences; none says that they were copied from castles.

sources.title: Bury St Edmunds Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: One of the best surviving examples of its type, this two-storey gate-hall is entered through a single archway which retains its portcullis.

sources.title: Thornton Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A bridge over the moat adjoins the gatehouse and is fortified with walls and garderobes.

links.claim: At the end of the Middle Ages gatehouses lost their defensive purpose and became grand entrances to manor houses; the Tudor great houses kept moats, gatehouses and crenellations to evoke the castle, their fortification largely symbolic.

sources.title: Gatehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By this time, the gatehouse had lost its defensive purpose and had become more of a monumental structure designed to harmonise with the manor or mansion.

sources.title: Tudor architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The residences of the king and nobility, while they had not been seriously defensible for centuries, still evoked the idea of the castle, with moats, gatehouses, machicolations and crenellations.

sources.title: Oxburgh Hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The gate was designed to evoke the owner's power and prestige, though as fortification its value is largely symbolic; it is flanked by tall polygonal towers rising in seven tiers, with symmetrical wings extending either side that reveal nothing on the exterior of their differing internal arrangements.

links.claim: Estate lodges are said to have originated from the gatehouses of medieval monasteries and manor houses, with the porter's lodge at Denbigh Castle and New College, Oxford, as antecedents; the lodge at the park gate took over the gatekeeper's work. The source gives the origin, not how or when the change came.

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Estate lodges originated from the gatehouses of medieval monasteries and manor houses.

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Timothy Mowl and Brian Earnshaw, in their study Trumpet at a Distant Gate: The Lodge as Prelude to the Country House, cite the Porter's Lodge Tower at Denbigh Castle, and the lodge at New College, Oxford as antecedent examples.

links.claim: Gate lodges became fashionable in the Georgian era along with landscape gardens and grew into a visual statement of the owner's taste. The source gives them as fashions of the same time, not a cause.

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They became fashionable in the Georgian era along with landscape gardens.

sources.title: Gate lodge
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Initially these lodges were functional wooden buildings, intended to retain livestock and deter intruders, but during the 18th century, they developed into a visual statement, designed to give an initial impression of the landowner's wealth and taste.

links.claim: Follies were an important feature of the English landscape garden of the 18th century, usually as Roman temples, ruined Gothic abbeys or pyramids; Kent's first garden at Chiswick already had a temple folly.

sources.title: Folly
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Follies in 18th-century French and English gardens"
sources.quote: Follies (French: fabriques) were an important feature of the English garden and French landscape garden in the 18th century, such as Stowe and Stourhead in England and Ermenonville and the gardens of Versailles in France.

sources.title: English landscape garden
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first gardens that he laid out between 1724 and 1733 had many formal elements of a garden à la française, including alleys forming a patte d'oie and canals, but they also featured a folly, a picturesque recreation of an Ionic temple set in a theatre of trees.

links.claim: A mews is a set of stables grouped round a yard or along a service street behind town houses, often with rooms above; the word was taken from the royal stables built on the king's hawk mews.

sources.title: Mews (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71774)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Traditionally a mew was a building housing hawks when they were moulting, however since the C16th the term has been used for a series of stables grouped around an open yard or alley, often with rooms above. Use only for stables otherwise use FALCONRY.

sources.title: Mews
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first recorded use meaning stables is dated 1548, after the royal stables were built at Charing Cross, on the site of the royal hawk mews.

links.claim: The coach house was built with the stables it served: in a mews the horse stalls and the carriage house share the ground floor. The sources show the two built together; none says that the coach house grew out of the stable.

sources.title: Mews
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The mews had horse stalls and a carriage house on the ground floor, and stable servants' living accommodation above.

sources.title: Mews
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A mews is a row or courtyard of stables and carriage houses with living quarters above them, built behind large city houses before motor vehicles replaced horses in the early twentieth century.

links.claim: The orangery began in the Renaissance gardens of Italy and spread north through the Netherlands and France; John Parkinson introduced it to English readers in 1628.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The orangery originated from the Renaissance gardens of Italy, when glass-making technology enabled sufficient expanses of clear glass to be produced.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the north, the Dutch led the way in developing expanses of window glass in orangeries, although the engravings illustrating Dutch manuals showed solid roofs, whether beamed or vaulted, and in providing stove heat rather than open fires.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In England, John Parkinson introduced the orangery to the readers of his Paradisus in Sole (1628), under the heading "Oranges".

links.claim: The orangery is a glasshouse for oranges and other non-hardy fruit trees, a large form of greenhouse; FISH places it under the glasshouse.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: An orangery or orangerie is a room or dedicated building, historically where orange and other non-hardy fruit trees are protected during the winter, as a large form of greenhouse or conservatory.

sources.title: Orangery (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69026)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.

links.claim: The conservatory grew out of the orangery: the houses for citrus trees widened their use to entertaining and other tender plants, sloped glass came in the 18th century and the glazed roof in the early 19th; today an orangery is told from a conservatory by having less of its roof glazed.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Orangeries, as they came to be called, were typically enclosed structures built with wood, brick or stone with tall vertical windows on the south walls.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Use of these rooms expanded socially and practically, being used to entertain and to host a wider variety of plants.

sources.title: Orangery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The glazed roof, which afforded sunlight to plants that were not dormant, was a development of the early 19th century.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In contemporary construction, a conservatory differs from an orangery in having more than 75% of its roof surface made from glass.

links.claim: A palm house is a conservatory tall enough for trees, for palms and tropical plants; the Victorian ones were of iron and glass.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Elsewhere, especially in America, it can often refer to a large freestanding glass-walled building in a botanic garden or park, sometimes also called a palm house if tall enough for trees.

sources.title: Palm House (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 92849)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A greenhouse used for growing palms and/or tropical plants.

sources.title: Conservatory (greenhouse)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Other examples include the Great Palm House at Kew Gardens that was built in 1844, built by Decimus Burton and the Crystal Palace, built for London's Great Exhibition of 1851 by Sir Joseph Paxton.

links.claim: Ice houses were brought to Britain by travellers who had seen Italian peasants keep mountain ice in caves; the first was James I's at Greenwich in 1619.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Ice houses were introduced to Britain by travellers who had seen similar arrangements in Italy, where peasants collected ice from the mountains and used it to keep food fresh in caves.

sources.title: Ice house (building)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The ice house was introduced to Britain in the 1600s.

links.claim: The mausoleum, named after the tomb of Mausolus, went out of use with Christianity; Hawksmoor revived it at Castle Howard (1729), designed after the Roman tomb of Caecilia Metella, almost certainly the first free-standing mausoleum in Western Europe since the fall of Rome.

sources.title: Mausoleum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The word mausoleum (from the Ancient Greek: μαυσωλεῖον) derives from the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus (near modern-day Bodrum in Turkey), the grave of King Mausolus, the Persian satrap of Caria, whose large tomb was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

sources.title: The Mausoleum, Castle Howard
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The mausoleum was designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor between 1726 and 1729, its design inspired by the Tomb of Caecilia Metella and the alleged Tomb of Lars Porsena.

sources.title: Nicholas Hawksmoor
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Mausoleum (1729–40) built on the same scale as his London churches, it is almost certainly the first free-standing mausoleum built in Western Europe since the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
